Physics project, 2024

Balloon Launch Camera Case

A case that held cameras on a weather balloon during the 2024 solar eclipse.

In April 2024, a group from DePaul's physics department traveled to Olney, Illinois, to watch the total solar eclipse. Some experiments stayed on the ground, and some went up on a weather balloon. My job was the equipment. We needed to record in three directions, and we needed to be able to turn the cameras on before launch.

I designed a three-part enclosure with camera mounts on the top, bottom, and middle. Four hollow tubes run along the corners of the case. Kevlar strings pass through these tubes, so the case can slide along the strings if the flight gets rough. Kevlar was chosen because it is very strong for its weight.

Raspberry Pi project

Real-Time Transit Display

A small screen that shows when the next Chicago bus or train is coming.

This display runs on a Raspberry Pi 4 with a 7-inch screen. It shows live arrival times for the bus and train routes you pick. It uses a web link from the Chicago Transit Authority (CTA), so it does not need a special key or account. The code can be changed to work with other transit systems.

I designed a 3D-printed case that holds the screen at a comfortable angle on a desk. There are two versions. One gives access to the Pi's connector pins, and the other is for display only.

Built with: Raspberry Pi 4, 7-inch display, 3D-printed case, Python

Light Scattering Test Bench

A test bench that moves a light detector to exact angles so experiments can be repeated.

Some experiments shine a laser through liquid containing small particles and measure the light that bounces off at different angles. This helps scientists learn the size of the particles. To check how well the measuring device works, the detector has to be moved to the same spots again and again. This bench does that using a motor, a gear, and limit switches.

Sample holder

The sample sits in a round glass tube so light can reach it from every direction. I designed a holder that keeps the tube centered on the same point the detector turns around. That way the sample stays in the same place at every angle.

Alignment pin

Lining up the laser with the sample is hard. I made a pin that fits into the holder and takes the sample's place. It has a thin piece in the middle that lights up when the laser hits it. This shows exactly where the beam is.

Centering cap

The turntable has a removable center piece. I designed a cap that fits in that spot and holds the sample post. This makes sure the sample is at the exact center of the turn.

Limit switches

Limit switches give the detector a starting point. Each test begins with the detector at home, out of the beam. The switch mount is held in two spots on the table so it does not shift when pushed from either direction.

Gear and motor

A motor turns a belt, and the belt turns a gear. The gear is attached to the big turntable. Because the gear has teeth, each step moves the turntable the same small amount every time. The gear is printed in six pieces that join with a dovetail, which is a sliding joint shaped like a tail. Glue can add extra hold over time.

Built with: 3D printing, stepper motor, Raspberry Pi Pico, limit switches, Python

3D-printed design

Boundary Line Winder

A compact winder that keeps beach volleyball boundary lines neat and easy to carry.

Most boundary line sets do not come with a way to wrap them up. I wanted something small and light, since I bike to the beach. The winder works for extension cords and other ropes too.

The first version was two printed pieces glued together, which worked for a few weeks until the frame bent and the pieces came apart. The second version uses a sliding dovetail joint to lock the pieces together, which made it much stronger.
